Based on my search, I can provide you with a comparison between the first satellite and modern satellites.

## Sputnik 1 (1957) - The First Artificial Satellite

**Sputnik 1**, launched by the Soviet Union on October 4, 1957, was humanity's first artificial satellite:

| Specification | Details |
|-------------|---------|
| **Diameter** | 58 cm (23 inches) |
| **Weight** | 83-84 kg |
| **Shape** | Metal sphere with four external antennas |
| **Orbit** | Elliptical: 230 km (perigee) to 940 km (apogee) |
| **Orbital period** | ~96 minutes |
| **Payload** | Thermometer, radio transmitter, batteries, fan |
| **Operational lifespan** | 3 weeks (batteries died) |
| **Total time in orbit** | ~3 months (burned up January 4, 1958) |

Sputnik 1 was extremely simple by today's standards—essentially a beeping radio transmitter in space. Its primary purpose was political and technological demonstration during the Cold War Space Race.

---

## Modern Satellites (2020s)

Today's satellites represent a quantum leap in complexity and capability:

| Type | Example | Weight | Capabilities |
|------|---------|--------|-------------|
| **Space Telescope** | Hubble Space Telescope | ~11,110 kg | Deep space observation, high-resolution imaging |
| **Communications Satellite** | Modern geostationary satellites | Up to ~7,000 kg | Global telecommunications, internet, broadcasting |
| **Space Station** | International Space Station | ~440,000 kg | Permanent human habitation, scientific research |
| **Earth Observation** | Modern imaging satellites | Varies widely | Sub-meter resolution, multispectral imaging, real-time data |
| **CubeSats/Miniaturized** | Various | 1-10 kg | Low-cost missions, technology demonstrations |

---

## Key Differences

| Aspect | Sputnik 1 (1957) | Modern Satellites |
|--------|---------------|-------------------|
| **Size/Scale** | Beach ball-sized | From smartphones to football-field-sized structures |
| **Weight** | 84 kg | Ranges from 1 kg (CubeSats) to 440,000 kg (ISS) |
| **Lifespan** | 3 weeks operational | 5-15+ years typical |
| **Power** | Batteries only | Solar panels, nuclear power, fuel cells |
| **Instruments** | Basic thermometer and radio | Advanced sensors, cameras, spectrometers, AI processing |
| **Data transmission** | Simple radio beeps | High-bandwidth laser communications, continuous streaming |
| **Navigation** | None | Precision station-keeping, autonomous maneuvering |
| **Purpose** | Political/technical demonstration | Communications, weather, navigation, science, military, internet |
| **Constellations** | Single satellite | Thousands working together (e.g., Starlink: 5,000+ satellites) |
| **Cost** | Relatively inexpensive | Millions to billions of dollars |

---

## The Evolution

The satellite revolution that began with Sputnik 1 has transformed every aspect of modern life. What started as a 23-inch metal sphere transmitting radio pulses has evolved into:

- **~8,000+ operational satellites** currently in orbit
- **Global positioning systems** (GPS, Galileo, BeiDou)
- **Real-time weather forecasting** and climate monitoring
- **Global internet connectivity** via mega-constellations
- **Military surveillance and communications**
- **Interplanetary probes** exploring distant worlds

The technological progress from Sputnik 1 to modern satellites spans roughly 67 years—less than a human lifetime—but represents one of the most dramatic technological leaps in history.

---

Sources:
1. https://astrobiology.nz/sputnik-1-and-the-space-age/
2. https://darwincav.com/sputnik-1-the-first-artificial-satellite/
